Chilean jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi) is a commercially important pelagic species whose early life history remains relatively understudied. During the initial stages of development, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges from a transparent pelagic egg with a diameter of approximately one millimeter. The recently eclosed prolarva, still dependent on endogenous yolk reserves, has a wet weight at birth of merely 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], reflecting the modest size of the fertilised ovum. At the thermal conditions typical of the species' spawning grounds, maintained at 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C], the time from fertilisation to the moment of larval eclosion spans approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days]. This relatively brief incubation period is consistent with observations in other carangid teleosts of similar egg size and is likely an adaptation to the dynamic, food-rich upwelling environments of the eastern South Pacific.

As the yolk-sac larva progresses through the lecithotrophic phase and transitions to active feeding, the subsequent juvenile period is marked by substantial somatic growth. Post-metamorphic individuals recruit to the pelagic juvenile stock and begin a rapid phase of mass increase that continues until the onset of sexual maturation. Field surveys and otolith-based back-calculation studies indicate that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the HPG axis, is attained at a total length of 40.5 centimeters [Lp = 40.5 centimeters]. This length serves as a reliable metric for identifying the transition from the immature, growing juvenile stage to a reproductively viable organism. The corresponding total body mass of the fish at this maturational threshold has been estimated at 1138 grams [Wwp = 1138 grams], a figure that reflects the substantial energetic investment required to reach reproductive competence in this fast-growing, iteroparous species.

During the adult phase, individuals of Trachurus murphyi continue to increase in size, albeit at a decelerating rate, until they approach their asymptotic dimensions. The ultimate total length recorded for this species reaches 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], a size that represents the maximum attainable under favourable environmental conditions and low fishing mortality. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fish of this length has been calculated at 5845 grams [Wwi = 5845 grams], a value derived from robust length-weight relationships established for the species across its geographic range. These figures place Chilean jack mackerel among the larger members of the genus Trachurus, consistent with the high productivity of the Humboldt Current system that supports its growth. The maximum recorded body mass highlights the species' capacity to achieve considerable size before the onset of senescence-related mortality.

Reproductive output in the Chilean jack mackerel is substantial, reflecting the species' importance as a small pelagic forage fish. Under the thermal regime of its subtropical spawning habitat, which remains consistently near 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate is high. This value is estimated through the combination of fecundity per spawning event and the frequency of those events. Available data for this species, informed by comparisons with the closely related congener Trachurus picturatus, indicate that a mature female releases approximately 828 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 828 eggs per spawning event], and that such spawning events can occur with a frequency of roughly one event per day [F_R_i = roughly one event per day] during the peak of the breeding season. This high instantaneous fecundity is a key life-history trait that underpins the population's resilience to exploitation.

The complete life cycle of the Chilean jack mackerel unfolds over a moderate time frame for a fish of its size, with longevity estimates constrained by both natural mortality and intense fishing pressure. Studies conducted under controlled conditions reflecting the species' typical environmental temperature of 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C] have documented a maximum lifespan of 16 years [am = 16 years]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately 5,840 days from the moment of gamete fusion to natural death, places T. murphyi among the longer-lived members of the Carangidae family, a lifespan that enables multiple reproductive seasons and a high cumulative lifetime fecundity. The combination of a moderately extended life span and extraordinarily high daily egg production creates a demographic profile well-suited to the variable but productive conditions of the southeast Pacific Ocean.
